text: Chapter 3 covered two release patterns, and rollback works differently in each one.

A blue-green rollback just flips routing back to blue, which never stopped running -- as fast as the original cutover. A rolling-update rollback runs the same process in reverse, instance by instance -- as gradual as the forward rollout was.

A fast rollback isn't automatic. It depends on the previous image tag still sitting in the registry, the previous config being recorded, and any new schema changes staying backward-compatible with the old code -- or the rollback breaks data.

An AI app has two separate things that can each go wrong: the application code, and the model or weights actually doing inference. A bad release can mean rolling back code only, model only, or both, tracked independently.

A thirty-second rollback is useless if the problem takes an hour to notice. The real first step is automated detection -- error rate, latency, and output quality signals -- wired to actually trigger the rollback.
That closes out deployment patterns. Chapter 4 picks up where this leaves off: scaling and reliability, starting with autoscaling AI workloads.
